evidence: Quint. 1.7.10: cum sit c littera, quae ad omnēs vōcālēs vim suam perferat
Cic. Div. 1.13.23: sūs rōstrō sī humī A litteram impresserit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: A written sign for a sound; in the plural also a letter (epistle) and literature. A word ends in a letter, in a litterā terminātur, with the letter’s name in apposition, as the Romans put it (Traupman 238; Quint. 1.5.62 nōn e litterā, sed tis syllabā). Capitals are litterae grandēs and small letters minūtae (Plautus, Lewis & Short; Traupman 245).

phrases.latin: hoc eō nōn omīsī, quod quīdam eam, quotiēns a sequātur, necessāriam crēdunt, cum sit c littera, quae ad omnēs vōcālēs vim suam perferat
phrases.english: I mention this because some think it necessary whenever a follows, though c is a letter that carries its sound to all the vowels

phrases.latin: retrō agant rūrsus et variā permūtātiōne turbent, dōnec litterās quī īnstituuntur faciē nōrint, nōn ōrdine
phrases.english: (teachers) take them back through the letters backwards and jumble them in all sorts of orders, until the learners know the letters by their look, not by their order

phrases.latin: eburneās etiam litterārum fōrmās in lūsum offerre
phrases.english: to give them letters made of ivory to play with

phrases.latin: ut puerīs ōlim dant crustula blandī doctōrēs, elementa velint ut discere prīma
phrases.english: as coaxing teachers sometimes give little boys biscuits, so that they will want to learn their ABC

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 238, 245, 247, 339.
